question: Which level of testing is specific to micro-frontend architecture and practically absent in a monolith?

options.text: Unit tests
options.explanation: Unit tests are used in any architecture — they test isolated components and are independent of architectural style.

options.text: Contract tests (Pact)
options.explanation: Consumer-driven contract testing solves the problem of independent deployments: it verifies that a change in one MFE does not break the expectations of another. In a monolith this is unnecessary — all components share common types.

options.text: E2E tests
options.explanation: E2E tests are used in monolithic architecture as well — they verify user scenarios regardless of the internal structure.

options.text: Visual regression
options.explanation: Visual regression tests are used in any frontend architecture. In MFE they are more important due to the risk of design desynchronization, but they are not unique to MFE.

question: How do you correctly stub an import from another MFE in Jest for unit tests?

options.text: Use jest.mock() with the full path to the remote
options.explanation: jest.mock('catalog/ProductList') does not work because Jest cannot resolve Module Federation remotes — this is a webpack runtime mechanism.

options.text: Configure moduleNameMapper in jest.config.ts
options.explanation: moduleNameMapper: { '^catalog/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/__mocks__/catalog/$1' } — the correct way. Jest intercepts the import during module resolution and substitutes a local mock file.

options.text: Start all MFE dev servers before tests
options.explanation: This is the approach for integration tests, not unit tests. Unit tests must work without network dependencies — fast and reliably.

options.text: Use jest.spyOn on the global __webpack_require__
options.explanation: Hacking webpack internals is a fragile approach that will break when tools are updated. moduleNameMapper is the official way.

question: In Pact, who generates the contract — consumer or provider?

options.text: Provider generates the contract, consumer verifies
options.explanation: This is the reverse order. The provider publishes an API but does not know all consumer expectations. The contract is formed from the side of the one who consumes.

options.text: Consumer generates the contract, provider verifies
options.explanation: Consumer-driven contract testing: Shell (consumer) runs the Pact test, which generates a pact.json with expectations. Catalog (provider) verifies that its API matches these expectations.

options.text: The contract is generated automatically from TypeScript types
options.explanation: TypeScript types are a compile-time artifact. Pact works with runtime HTTP interactions and has no knowledge of TypeScript.

options.text: Both generate their parts independently
options.explanation: This is not a consumer-driven approach. The essence of Pact is that the consumer dictates expectations and the provider must satisfy them.

question: You have 5 MFEs and the E2E test pipeline takes 50 minutes. Which approach is most effective?

options.text: Run E2E only on a pre-release tag, not on every PR
options.explanation: Slow tests should not block every PR. Unit + Contract on PR, E2E — before deploying to production.

options.text: Use Playwright sharding: --shard=1/5 for parallelization
options.explanation: Playwright supports sharding — splitting tests across N parallel agents. 50 min / 5 = ~10 min per shard.

options.text: Remove Visual regression tests entirely
options.explanation: Visual regression tests are important when working with a design system. It is better to optimize the run (only changed MFEs) than to remove them.

options.text: Keep only smoke tests for E2E, give detailed coverage to integration
options.explanation: E2E should cover only critical user journeys (3–5 scenarios). Detailed behavior is tested at the integration level, which is faster.

question: What is a mock remote in the context of MFE testing?

options.text: A Jest mock for functions inside an MFE
options.explanation: A Jest mock is a unit-testing tool for stubbing functions. A mock remote is an architectural pattern at the Module Federation level.

options.text: A replacement of a real MFE with a simplified stub in the Module Federation config
options.explanation: A mock remote is a separate webpack bundle that exports the same modules as the real MFE, but with predictable behavior. Shell connects it instead of the real remote during testing.

options.text: An HTTP mock server intercepting requests to the MFE
options.explanation: An HTTP mock (MSW) intercepts API requests but does not replace the MFE itself as a Module Federation remote.

options.text: Storybook with isolated MFE components
options.explanation: Storybook is a component development tool. A mock remote is a specific pattern for substituting a Module Federation remote in a test configuration.

question: A team updates design tokens (colors, spacing) in a shared design system. Which type of tests will be the first to catch visual desynchronizations between MFEs?

options.text: Unit tests of components
options.explanation: Unit tests check logic and rendering, not visual correspondence. Changing a CSS variable will not break a unit test.

options.text: Contract tests
options.explanation: Contract tests verify API contracts, not visuals. Pact has no knowledge of CSS.

options.text: Visual regression tests
options.explanation: This is exactly what visual regression tests exist for. When a design token is updated, each MFE's snapshot will change and the test will fail — the team will see all discrepancies before deployment.

options.text: Integration tests
options.explanation: Integration tests verify MFE interaction (EventBus, state), not CSS/visuals.

question: What is 'Can I Deploy' in the context of Pact?

options.text: A CI/CD command to check infrastructure readiness
options.explanation: This is not an infrastructure check — it is a Pact Broker tool.

options.text: A Pact Broker tool that checks whether an MFE version is compatible with all consumer contracts before deployment
options.explanation: npx pact-broker can-i-deploy --pacticipant CatalogMFE --version X queries the Pact Broker: 'Are there any unverified contracts for this version?' If yes — deployment is blocked.

options.text: A check for whether a developer has deployment permissions
options.explanation: This is not about access rights. Can I Deploy is exclusively about contract compatibility between MFEs.

options.text: A command to run E2E tests before deployment
options.explanation: E2E tests run separately. Can I Deploy is a Pact-specific tool for checking contract compatibility.

question: What CI trigger is optimal for a full E2E + Visual regression suite in a large MFE system?

options.text: Every commit to a feature branch
options.explanation: Too expensive — developers wait 40+ minutes for every commit. This kills productivity.

options.text: Every PR to main
options.explanation: Unit + Contract are suitable for every PR, but full E2E + Visual is too slow and expensive for the PR cycle.

options.text: Pre-release tag (before deploying to production)
options.explanation: The optimal balance: developers do not wait in PRs, but a full check runs before an actual deployment. A nightly run can also be added for early problem detection.

options.text: Manual trigger only
options.explanation: A manual trigger creates risk: someone will forget to run the tests. Automation on pre-release is more reliable.

question: A team is working on Cart MFE. Catalog MFE changed the structure of its exported data: { products: [] } → { items: [] }. Which test will catch this earliest?

options.text: Unit test of Cart MFE
options.explanation: Cart's unit test works with a mock Catalog. If the mock is not updated — the test will pass, but prod will break.

options.text: Contract test (Pact) for Shell → Catalog
options.explanation: Shell's Pact test fixes the expectation { products: [] }. When verifying the new Catalog v1.6 with { items: [] }, the test will fail and can-i-deploy will block the deployment.

options.text: E2E test of checkout flow
options.explanation: E2E will catch it, but later — you have to wait for the E2E pipeline to run. A contract test catches it immediately when attempting to deploy Catalog.

options.text: TypeScript compilation in the Shell repository
options.explanation: Shell and Catalog are separate repositories. Shell's TypeScript has no knowledge of a runtime change in Catalog until the remote is loaded in the browser.

question: You are setting up a hybrid mock strategy. Which configuration is correct?

options.text: All remotes are mocked, except the MFE under test
options.explanation: Hybrid: the MFE under test is real (to verify its behavior), all dependencies are mocked (to isolate from external changes). This is the optimal balance of speed and fidelity.

options.text: All remotes are real dev servers
options.explanation: This is 'real remotes', not hybrid. It requires all MFEs to run simultaneously — slow and unstable.

options.text: All remotes are mocked, including the one under test
options.explanation: If the MFE under test is also mocked — what exactly are we testing? This makes no sense.

options.text: Only APIs are mocked, all MFEs are real
options.explanation: This is the MSW approach (mocking HTTP), not the mock remote strategy. Mock remote replaces the MFE as a Module Federation remote, not the API.

question: What attributes are recommended to add to MFE root elements for easy testing?

options.text: data-mfe="catalog" to identify the MFE in E2E tests
options.explanation: data-mfe allows E2E tests to unambiguously find the MFE boundary: page.locator('[data-mfe="catalog"]'). This is a stable selector that does not depend on CSS.

options.text: data-testid with a unique MFE prefix (catalog-search, cart-total)
options.explanation: A prefix prevents conflicts between MFEs. cart-total and catalog-total are different elements — the test unambiguously knows which MFE to look in.

options.text: CSS class and id for stable selectors
options.explanation: CSS classes are an implementation detail. They change when styles are refactored. data-testid intentionally carries no style load and is more stable.

options.text: aria-label for accessibility, which is also used in tests
options.explanation: Using aria-label/aria-role in tests is good practice: tests verify accessibility alongside functionality. getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }) is a reliable selector.

question: A team has added a new 'Reviews' MFE. Unit tests are written. What else must be done before other MFEs start using Reviews?

options.text: Write a Pact consumer test for each MFE that will use Reviews
options.explanation: Each consumer (Shell, Catalog) must fix its expectations for Reviews through Pact. Without this, there is no guarantee of compatibility during independent deployments.

options.text: Set up a Visual baseline for the Reviews MFE
options.explanation: The first run of Playwright with --update-snapshots creates the baseline. Without it, visual regression tests have nothing to compare against.

options.text: Add Reviews to the E2E test matrix
options.explanation: Not mandatory right away — E2E covers critical user journeys, not every possible scenario. Adding Reviews to integration tests is sufficient.

options.text: Add a mock for Reviews in the moduleNameMapper of other MFEs
options.explanation: Other MFEs that will import from Reviews must have a mock in their Jest configuration for unit tests.

question: A visual regression test unexpectedly failed due to a button animation (a different screenshot frame). How should this be fixed correctly?

options.text: Increase the wait timeout to 10 seconds
options.explanation: A timeout does not solve the animation problem — the screenshot will still capture an arbitrary frame.

options.text: Use the mask option or disable animations via a CSS media query in tests
options.explanation: Playwright supports mask to hide dynamic areas. You can also emulate prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, which causes most CSS animations to complete instantly.

options.text: Delete the visual regression test for this component
options.explanation: Deletion is a last resort. The flakiness should first be fixed rather than abandoning the test.

options.text: Increase maxDiffPixelRatio to 50%
options.explanation: A 50% tolerance makes the test meaningless — it will miss real visual regressions. The normal range is 1–5%.

question: Why can't you rely solely on TypeScript to verify cross-team contracts in MFE architecture?

options.text: TypeScript does not support Module Federation
options.explanation: TypeScript supports Module Federation via @module-federation/typescript or manual type declarations. This is not a problem.

options.text: TypeScript checks types at compile time, but MFEs deploy independently — the runtime version may differ from the types in another repository
options.explanation: Shell is compiled with Catalog v1.5 types. But in production, Catalog v1.6 with a changed API may be deployed. TypeScript will not protect against this runtime mismatch. Pact verifies real HTTP interactions.

options.text: TypeScript compiles too slowly in a monorepo
options.explanation: Compilation performance is a separate issue, unrelated to contract testing.

options.text: Module Federation does not support strict TypeScript
options.explanation: This is incorrect. TypeScript strict mode works with Module Federation.

question: Which statement about the ratio of testing levels in an MFE system is most correct?

options.text: Even distribution: 20% unit, 20% contract, 20% integration, 20% e2e, 20% visual
options.explanation: An even distribution violates the pyramid principle. E2E and visual are expensive — there should be fewer of them. Unit tests are cheap — there should be more of them.

options.text: Foundation — unit (~70%), middle layer — contract + integration (~20%), top — e2e + visual (~10%)
options.explanation: This is the classic testing pyramid adapted for MFE. Unit tests are cheap and fast — there are many. E2E and visual are expensive, slow, and fragile — there are few, covering only critical scenarios.

options.text: Foundation — e2e (70%), because they verify real UX
options.explanation: This is an inverted pyramid (the ice cream cone anti-pattern). E2E tests are slow, expensive, and unstable — they should not be the majority.

options.text: Contract tests should make up 50%+ for MFE, other levels are secondary
options.explanation: Contract tests are important for MFE, but they do not replace other levels. Unit tests cover the internal component logic that Pact does not test.
